source.title: Sparse autoencoders find composed features in small toy models

record.tranche_reason: The post reports results about sparse autoencoders recovering composed feature directions in toy models, not mixed responses of individual neurons in trained networks or the rate of polysemantic neurons. Its results therefore do not test a listed version of the claim.
record.gate_note: The post measures SAE feature recovery and toy-model feature geometry. These are related to interpretability and feature composition, but are not the neuron-response behavior specified by the claim versions; results are recorded under fits_no_version. The post also mentions earlier findings from other work, which are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The post trains SAEs on a 2-dimensional linear hidden layer of a ReLU-output toy model. It asks whether SAE latents recover the stipulated features or composed pairs. The toy model's hidden layer has no activation function, so it has no privileged basis and no neurons whose polysemanticity could be measured. The SAE latents are a dictionary-learning tool, not neurons of a trained classifier or language model. None of V1–V7 is tested. The superposition result (r1) concerns feature directions, not neuron responses, so it fits no version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that SAEs find composed rather than true features in this toy setup, even with 75% one-hot data. In the comments, the lead author accepts that the first dataset's true features were the diagonals and that the second dataset's principal components explain the result.
record.recipe_differences: The post trains SAEs on synthetic data and a two-hidden-dimension ReLU output toy model; it does not use the neuron-response measurement in the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: SAE outcomes varied with feature-amplitude correlation, learning rate, ℓ1 coefficient, realization, one-hot data probability, and the form of the cosine-similarity penalty.

fits_no_version.finding: A 2-hidden-dimension toy model stores four anticorrelated features as antipodal pairs in superposition. The features occur every other draw.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Toy models can place more features than dimensions in superposition when the features are anticorrelated, even when each feature is not rare.

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs on the toy hidden activations mostly learn composed-pair directions rather than the stipulated features. This holds across learning rate, λ, cosine penalties and 75% one-hot data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents can recover composed or rotated feature directions rather than the stipulated underlying features in small toy settings.

record.problems: The study uses an extremely small, synthetic setup with two feature sets of two features. The post itself calls the correlated-amplitude case contrived. In the comments, the authors agree that the first dataset did not have the intended underlying features and acknowledge that the second dataset's principal directions may explain the SAE results; the authors say the setup may not be the best way to study the phenomenon. Numerical outcome tables and uncertainty estimates are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result was left out. The post mentions p(one-hot)=0.5 but says results are displayed only for p(one-hot)=0.75, so no separate outcome row is available for 0.5.

untested.parts: No image classifiers or their neurons are studied.
No transformer language models or MLP neurons are studied.
No neurons with a privileged basis. Superposition is shown only for directions in a linear 2-D hidden space.
No test of neuron polysemanticity without capacity pressure.
No comparison of the polysemantic neuron share across activations, architectures or regularization.
No canonical polysemantic neurons are re-examined.
No comparison of neuron polysemanticity measures. The SAE monosemanticity score is used only on SAE latents.

record.verdict_notes: Commenters (LawrenceC, Ali Shehper) argue the 'composed' directions are the data's principal directions or an equally valid basis. The lead author largely agrees, which weakens the failure-mode framing. The study is not one of the original sources. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: No image-classifier neurons or their responses are studied.
No transformer language models, MLP neurons, or language contexts are studied.
The post studies SAE feature recovery and toy-model superposition, not whether individual neurons are polysemantic because of capacity pressure.
The post does not test polysemantic neurons without capacity pressure or attribute them to initialization, regularization, or training noise.
It does not measure the share of polysemantic neurons across architectures, activations, or regularization settings, or compare that share with performance.
The discussion of alternative bases and principal directions concerns SAE features in toy data, not whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect one shared feature.
It does not compare ways of measuring or scoring neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: ReLU output toy model (2 hidden dimensions)
rows.operation_detail: Trained a toy model to reconstruct synthetic composed-feature inputs.
rows.value: The model stores the features in superposition using antipodal feature pairs, despite each feature occurring in every other data vector on average.
rows.note: The post describes toy-model feature storage, not the response of individual neurons.
rows.check: Linking to none is correct. The hidden layer h=Wx is linear and non-privileged, so 'superposition' here describes feature directions, not polysemantic neurons. It cannot bear on V3.

rows.subject: Sparse autoencoders trained on the ReLU output toy model
rows.operation_detail: Trained five SAE realizations on toy-model hidden activations.
rows.measure: Whether SAE features match the stipulated underlying features or encode composed pairs
rows.value: All five realizations showed the composed-feature issue; only one realization found even a single true underlying feature.

conditions.value: two orders of magnitude in each

rows.value: Only one hyperparameter setting produced a mostly monosemantic realization; it was not perfectly monosemantic.

rows.subject: Sparse autoencoders trained on the ReLU output toy model
rows.operation_detail: Trained SAEs on toy-model hidden activations with uncorrelated feature amplitudes.
rows.measure: Whether SAE features encode composed pairs or the stipulated underlying features
rows.value: SAEs almost uniformly learned perfect composed pairs across the parameters studied. Some realizations at high learning rate and low λ found monosemantic features, but other realizations had lower loss and composed features.
rows.note: The report distinguishes lower-loss composed-feature realizations from some monosemantic realizations.
rows.check: The post calls composed-pair SAE latents 'polysemantic realizations'. These are SAE dictionary features, not model neurons, so they do not bear on V2, V5 or V7.

rows.subject: Sparse autoencoders trained on the ReLU output toy model
rows.operation_detail: Added a mean of decoder-column cosine similarities to the SAE loss.

rows.baseline: SAE setup without the added cosine term
rows.value: The post reports that the models found the same solution as before; the added term did not improve monosemantic feature recovery.

relation.reason: The post discusses superposition and SAE feature recovery, and uses 'polysemantic' only for SAE latents; it does not test the claim.

tranche.reason: SAE training on a linear-hidden-layer toy model (h=Wx); no privileged basis or neurons, so no test of any polysemantic-neuron version.

source_check.notes: The first dataset's true features were actually the diagonals, and the second's principal components explain the SAE result. The lead author concedes both in the comments. The rows record only the post's original claims. SAE dictionary size F is never stated; monosemanticity uses Eqn. 7 of Jermyn et al. 2022.
